1.QUESTION: A 30-year-old man with a family history of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) undergoes renal ultrasound screening. How many cysts are required to make a diagnosis at his age according to the Unified Ultrasound Diagnostic Criteria?

OPTION.A: At least 1 cyst in one kidney
OPTION.D: At least 2 cysts in each kidney
OPTION.E: At least 4 cysts in each kidney

1.EXPLANATION: For at-risk individuals aged 15-39 years, the Unified Ultrasound Diagnostic Criteria require at least 3 cysts (unilateral or bilateral). For ages 40-59: at least 2 in each kidney; for age ≥60: at least 4 in each kidney.

2.QUESTION: Which genetic mutation in ADPKD is associated with a more severe phenotype and earlier onset of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD)?
2.EXPLANATION: PKD1 mutations account for ~85% of ADPKD and cause more severe disease, with average ESKD onset at ~57 years. PKD2 mutations (15%) are milder (ESKD ~74 years). PKHD1 causes ARPKD.

3.QUESTION: A 38-year-old man with a strong family history of ADPKD undergoes renal ultrasound as part of a routine screening. He has no symptoms, and his serum creatinine is normal. The ultrasound shows a single 0.8 cm cyst in the left kidney and no cysts in the right kidney. According to the Unified Ultrasound Diagnostic Criteria, what is the most appropriate interpretation?

OPTION.A: Diagnostic of ADPKD because any cyst in an at-risk individual is abnormal.
OPTION.B: Indeterminate; requires repeat ultrasound in 2 years.
OPTION.C: Normal; ADPKD is excluded because he is over 30 and has fewer than 3 cysts.
OPTION.D: Suggests a different cystic disease; order genetic testing immediately.
OPTION.E: Diagnostic of ADPKD; start tolvaptan therapy.

3.EXPLANATION: For at-risk individuals aged 15-39 years, the Unified Ultrasound Diagnostic Criteria require at least 3 cysts (unilateral or bilateral) to diagnose ADPKD. A single cyst at age 38 does not meet the criteria and essentially excludes ADPKD. Normal ultrasound at age 40 or older has a high negative predictive value.

4.QUESTION: What is the mechanism of action of tolvaptan in the treatment of ADPKD?
4.EXPLANATION: Tolvaptan is a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist. It reduces cAMP‑driven cyst cell proliferation and fluid secretion, slowing kidney cyst growth and function decline.

5.QUESTION: A 33-year-old woman with ADPKD and polycystic liver disease has had two episodes of cyst infection in the past year. She is planning to start a family. Which of the following statements regarding pregnancy and disease management is most accurate?

OPTION.A: Pregnancy is contraindicated in ADPKD because of high risk of uterine rupture.
OPTION.B: Multiple pregnancies are associated with accelerated growth of liver cysts.
OPTION.C: Tolvaptan is safe and recommended throughout pregnancy to slow cyst growth.
OPTION.D: Estrogen-containing contraceptives are preferred to reduce cyst infection risk.
OPTION.E: ADPKD is not inherited, so there is no risk to the offspring.

5.EXPLANATION: In ADPKD, polycystic liver disease is often more severe in women, especially with multiparity and estrogen exposure. Multiple pregnancies can accelerate liver cyst growth. Pregnancy itself is not contraindicated but requires monitoring. Tolvaptan is teratogenic and not used in pregnancy. Progesterone-only contraceptives are preferred.

6.QUESTION: A 45-year-old man with ADPKD presents with acute, severe flank pain and gross hematuria. He is afebrile and hemodynamically stable. What is the most likely cause?
6.EXPLANATION: Acute flank pain with gross hematuria in ADPKD is most often due to cyst hemorrhage. Management is conservative with hydration and analgesics; hemorrhage typically resolves spontaneously within days to weeks.

7.QUESTION: A known ADPKD patient develops fever, flank pain, and tenderness over a renal cyst. Urinalysis is negative for infection. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate antibiotic class?

OPTION.B: Cyst infection; treat with lipophilic antibiotics (e.g., fluoroquinolone)
OPTION.D: Renal cell carcinoma; treat with nephrectomy

7.EXPLANATION: Suspect cyst infection when fever and flank pain are present. Urine culture may be negative because infected cysts may not communicate with the collecting system. Treatment requires lipophilic antibiotics (e.g., fluoroquinolones, TMP‑SMX) that penetrate cyst walls.

8.QUESTION: A 42-year-old man with ADPKD has persistent hypertension despite lifestyle modifications. His office blood pressure is 135/85 mm Hg on two separate occasions. According to the 2025 KDIGO guidelines, what is the recommended target systolic blood pressure and initial pharmacologic therapy?

OPTION.A: Target SBP <130 mm Hg; start amlodipine.
OPTION.B: Target SBP <120 mm Hg; start lisinopril.
OPTION.C: Target SBP <140 mm Hg; start hydrochlorothiazide.
OPTION.D: Target SBP <120 mm Hg; start metoprolol.
OPTION.E: Target SBP <130 mm Hg; start doxazosin.

8.EXPLANATION: KDIGO 2025 recommends a systolic BP target of <120 mm Hg for ADPKD patients. First-line therapy is a RAAS inhibitor (ACE inhibitor or ARB). Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor. Amlodipine (CCB) and metoprolol (beta-blocker) are not first-line. Thiazides are not preferred for initial monotherapy in ADPKD.

9.QUESTION: A 35-year-old woman with ADPKD has a family history of cerebral aneurysm rupture. She is a commercial airline pilot. What is the recommended screening approach for intracranial aneurysms?

OPTION.A: No screening because she is under 40
OPTION.B: Routine screening of all ADPKD patients with CT angiography
OPTION.C: MRA screening because of family history and high‑risk profession
OPTION.E: Screening only if she develops severe headache

9.EXPLANATION: KDIGO guidelines recommend screening for cerebral aneurysms (MRA) in ADPKD patients with a family history of aneurysms or sudden death, or those in high‑risk professions (e.g., pilots). Routine screening of all ADPKD patients is not advised.

10.QUESTION: A 25-year-old man is found to have multiple bilateral renal cysts on ultrasound. He has no family history of kidney disease, and his parents are in their 60s with normal renal ultrasound. What is the most appropriate next step?

OPTION.A: Diagnose ADPKD based on cyst count alone
OPTION.B: Perform genetic testing for PKD1 and PKD2
OPTION.E: Order MRI to confirm cyst number

10.EXPLANATION: Genetic testing is recommended in ambiguous cases, such as young patients without a clear family history, equivocal imaging, or when a de novo mutation is suspected. It provides diagnostic and prognostic information.

11.QUESTION: A 50-year-old patient with ADPKD has an eGFR of 30 mL/min/1.73m² and a Mayo classification of 1D (rapid progressor). Which drug is indicated to slow disease progression?
11.EXPLANATION: Tolvaptan is indicated for adults with eGFR ≥25 mL/min/1.73m² who are at risk of rapid progression (Mayo class 1C‑E or rapid eGFR decline). It is the only FDA‑approved disease‑modifying therapy for ADPKD.

12.QUESTION: A 60-year-old patient with ADPKD has an eGFR of 15 mL/min/1.73m² and massive hepatomegaly from polycystic liver disease. Which symptom is most likely related to the liver cysts?
12.EXPLANATION: Polycystic liver disease can cause massive hepatomegaly, leading to early satiety, abdominal discomfort, and pain. Flank pain and hematuria are renal; cerebral aneurysm and MVP are other extrarenal but not caused by liver cysts.

13.QUESTION: A 55-year-old woman with ADPKD has an eGFR of 22 mL/min/1.73m² and a height-adjusted total kidney volume (htTKV) that places her in Mayo class 1D (rapid progressor). She is being evaluated for tolvaptan. Which of the following is a required monitoring parameter during tolvaptan therapy?

OPTION.A: Monthly serum potassium for the first 6 months
OPTION.B: Monthly liver function tests for the first 18 months

13.EXPLANATION: Tolvaptan can cause hepatotoxicity. Liver enzymes must be monitored monthly for the first 18 months of therapy, then every 3 months thereafter. Potassium monitoring is not specific to tolvaptan. Cerebral MRA is not routine. Echocardiograms and daily proteinuria are not required.

14.QUESTION: Which of the following is the most common extrarenal manifestation of ADPKD, affecting up to 90% of patients by age 35?
14.EXPLANATION: Polycystic liver disease is the most common extrarenal manifestation, occurring in up to 90% of ADPKD patients by age 35. It is often asymptomatic but can cause massive hepatomegaly.

15.QUESTION: A 32-year-old woman with ADPKD presents with a sudden, severe headache described as 'the worst headache of my life.' What is the most important immediate diagnostic step?

OPTION.B: Non‑contrast head CT or MRA to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage

15.EXPLANATION: Sudden severe headache in ADPKD is a neurologic emergency until a ruptured cerebral aneurysm is excluded. Non‑contrast head CT or MRA is the appropriate initial imaging.

16.QUESTION: A 40-year-old man with ADPKD has a serum creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL and an eGFR of 85 mL/min/1.73m². His renal ultrasound shows multiple cysts bilaterally. He has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate management at this stage?

OPTION.C: Blood pressure control, hydration, and annual monitoring
OPTION.E: Start chronic NSAIDs for pain prophylaxis

16.EXPLANATION: Early management focuses on blood pressure control, high water intake, sodium restriction, and regular monitoring. Tolvaptan is reserved for patients with rapid progression and eGFR ≥25.

17.QUESTION: A 55-year-old ADPKD patient is found to have an eGFR decline of 5 mL/min/1.73m² per year over the past 2 years. According to guidelines, what is the primary indication for tolvaptan therapy?

OPTION.A: Any patient with ADPKD regardless of eGFR
OPTION.C: eGFR ≥25 mL/min/1.73m² and risk of rapid progression (e.g., eGFR decline >3 mL/min/year)

17.EXPLANATION: Tolvaptan is indicated for adults with eGFR ≥25 mL/min/1.73m² who are at risk of rapid progression, defined as Mayo class 1C‑E or a confirmed annual eGFR decline of ≥3 mL/min/1.73m².

18.QUESTION: A 2‑year‑old child presents with massive bilateral renal enlargement, hypertension, and signs of congenital hepatic fibrosis. Which genetic disorder is most likely?
18.EXPLANATION: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is caused by PKHD1 mutations and typically presents in infancy or early childhood with massive renal enlargement and congenital hepatic fibrosis.

19.QUESTION: A 47-year-old man with ADPKD presents with a 2-day history of right flank pain, fever (38.9°C), and chills. He has had several similar episodes in the past that resolved with oral antibiotics. Physical examination reveals marked tenderness over the right kidney. Urinalysis shows no leukocytes or nitrites. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

OPTION.B: Intravenous or oral lipophilic antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin)
OPTION.E: Observation without antibiotics because urine is sterile

19.EXPLANATION: This presentation is classic for cyst infection in ADPKD. Urine culture may be negative because infected cysts often do not communicate with the collecting system. Treatment requires lipophilic antibiotics that penetrate the cyst wall (fluoroquinolones, TMP-SMX). Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate cyst penetration. Surgery is not first-line. Cyst aspiration is reserved for failure of medical therapy.

20.QUESTION: A 58-year-old man with ADPKD and a living related kidney donor is being prepared for preemptive kidney transplantation. He has massive bilateral renal enlargement with chronic pain and two episodes of cyst infection in the past year. Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical approach before transplantation?

OPTION.E: No native kidney surgery; proceed directly to transplant

20.EXPLANATION: In ADPKD patients with recurrent cyst infections, severe pain, or massive enlargement that impairs nutrition or mobility, native nephrectomy is indicated before or at the time of kidney transplantation. Prophylactic aneurysm clipping is not indicated without known aneurysm. Liver cyst surgery is for symptomatic PLD. Partial decortication is not standard. Doing nothing risks post-transplant complications from infected native kidneys.
